messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luka fled his home country at age eleven, when soldiers swept through his village and he spent six hours hidden in a root cellar while his mother pressed her hand over his mouth. Through a crack in the wooden door he watched a neighbor crawl across the yard and then stop moving. That image, the color of her dress against the mud, has stayed with him as a series of still pictures that arrive without warning. Sometimes when a memory comes, he finds his body frozen in the same curled position he held in that cellar, knees to chest, shoulders tight, as if the floorboards beneath his office chair might split open at any moment. More disturbing are the episodes where the full terror of that afternoon floods through him—racing heart, sweaty palms, the certainty of imminent death—without any image attached, leaving him disoriented and ashamed.

Luka works as a public defender, a job he chose because he wanted to stand up for people who had no one, but the content of his cases is a constant, low-grade trigger. On his first day in the courtroom, a door slammed and he dove sideways in his chair. Now he startles at ordinary sounds—the clatter of a coffee mug, the squeak of a cart in the hallway—and each time his body reacts before his mind can catch up. Unusual silence is worse: when the bustle of the courthouse suddenly quiets, he feels something dangerous is about to happen, as if the world has drawn a breath before striking. He often reacts as though he is in real danger when nothing is actually wrong, and afterward he has to sit in his car for ten minutes to calm down. Each time his body floods with that false alarm, it feels like fresh proof that danger really is everywhere, and the belief that he must constantly be on guard hardens a little more.

Luka has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place and that he has to be on guard all the time. He tells himself he must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Because of this constant vigilance, he carefully monitors his own thoughts for signs that he is going crazy—he checks whether his mind is drifting toward the event, whether his fear is irrational, whether he is about to lose control. He refuses to talk with anyone about what happened, not even his girlfriend, Maya. When colleagues bring up work that reminds him of the event—a case about a refugee family, or a client who fled violence—he changes the subject or walks away. But this avoidance only deepens his conviction that the world is unsafe; without ever discussing his experiences, he cannot test whether his fears are accurate, so every unspoken thought becomes further evidence of danger. This conviction that the world is dangerous keeps dragging him back to the cellar—as if his mind needs to confirm the source of its fear, the memory of the neighbor's dress or the soldier's boots rises up to meet his belief, vivid and waiting.

The intrusive memories themselves reinforce his sense that the world is dangerous. When a visual memory strikes—the neighbor’s dress, the crack in the door, the soldier’s boots—his body goes straight into threat mode: he startles, his pulse pounds, and he feels again that he is about to die. In turn, each false alarm or startle reaction triggers a memory: a sudden loud sound will pull him back to the night of the raid, and he will feel the cold dirt floor beneath him and hear his mother’s whisper. The cycle tightens: feeling threatened makes him more vigilant and more avoidant, and each attempt to escape the memories only reinforces his belief that he must remain on guard.

Luka’s relationship with Maya has become strained. She wants to know why he never talks about his past, why he flinches when she touches him unexpectedly. He cannot explain it. In court last week, a client’s testimony about hiding during a bombing sent Luka into a dissociative fog; he could not speak for two minutes. That afternoon, his supervising attorney told him his performance was slipping and asked if he needed leave. Luka has finally scheduled an appointment with a therapist, but what frightens him most is the thought that talking about the trauma will make him fall apart completely. He is hoping the therapist can help him stop feeling so constantly afraid, but he is terrified of what he might discover inside his own mind.
